design_detail: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42021293500; Cochrane Handbook methods; GRADE certainty ratings) of human studies of cancer incidence, cancer-specific mortality and survival after a cancer diagnosis in people who use Swedish snus and no other tobacco, against people who never used tobacco. Search run in May 2022. 15 studies met the criteria (14 cohort studies, 1 case-control study), almost all in men and most drawing on the same Swedish construction-worker cohort. Results are given study by study; the only pooling is a two-study inverse-variance combination for rectal cancer. Studies by researchers linked to, or sponsored by, the tobacco industry were excluded by design.
can_establish: What the published cohort and case-control studies up to May 2022 found, cancer site by cancer site, about cancer and cancer death in men who use snus and nothing else against men who never used tobacco, and how confident the reviewers were in each graded estimate.
cannot_establish: Causation (all evidence is observational); anything about women (almost no data); how snus compares with smoking (a descriptive collation of separate studies, not a pooled comparison, and its figure was not read as numbers here); rare cancers (few events); risks at older ages (few snus-using men were followed past 70); other smokeless products or nicotine pouches; or independent replication (most estimates come from one cohort, the Construction Workers Cohort, or from pooled analyses that contain it).

sample.recruitment: Search of the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), PsycInfo, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials and Web of Science in May 2022 by a head librarian, building on searches run in 2004, 2013 and 2018 at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health; geographic terms restricted the search to Swedish snus; reference lists of included studies were screened. English, Norwegian, Swedish and Danish only. Search strategy in Table S1 (supplement, not read) (Methods › 2.2 Search strategy).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human studies of any design reporting cancer risk, total mortality or cancer-specific mortality for people who use snus exclusively against people who never used tobacco; current use at baseline preferred where available. Excluded: estimates based only on combined snus and cigarette use, and studies by researchers with links to the tobacco industry or sponsored by it (Methods › 2.3 Study eligibility criteria). Exclusion reasons are in Table S4 (not read).
sample.demographics: Almost all men. Only one of the 15 studies gave any estimate for women (lymphoma, with no cases among women). More than 75% of the men using snus only in the construction-worker cohort were under 30 at entry, and few were followed beyond 70 (Discussion › 4.2, 3rd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Restricting to snus-only against never-tobacco removes confounding by smoking but also removes everyone who used both, so the review says nothing about dual use. Excluding industry-linked studies is a stated choice. One cohort dominates: in the pooled nine-cohort analysis, two thirds of participants and 72% of pancreatic cancer cases or deaths came from the Construction Workers Cohort (Results › 3.1.4, 2nd paragraph). When several studies drew on the same population, the one with most participants or longest follow-up was graded (Methods › 2.6).

exposure.measurement: Whatever the primary studies recorded: a single self-report of tobacco habits at baseline in the Swedish cohorts, with current use at baseline preferred. The authors note that the single recording, with young participants at baseline and cancer appearing mostly after 50, leaves the estimates open to later changes in habit; one Swedish study found that about 30% of men using snus only may later stop or switch to smoking (Discussion › 4.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesised. Some primary studies report amount or duration (for example colorectal cancer at seven cans or more a week, hazard ratio 1.36, 1.04 to 1.78; Hodgkin lymphoma after more than 30 years, incidence rate ratio 3.78, 1.23 to 11.60, 4 exposed cases) (Results › 3.1.5, 3.1.7). Route: oral.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled by design: only snus-only men against men who never used tobacco were graded, because adjusting for smoking in samples that included people who smoke and people who used both distorted snus estimates in one study (Discussion › 4.1, 1st paragraph). Residual smoking in the snus-only group is possible: in one study 13.2% of never-smoking men using snus had at least one repeat record showing smoking, against 6.7% of men who never used tobacco (Discussion › 4.2, 5th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Former use was not graded; the authors chose current use at baseline to avoid uncertainty about duration, dose and changes in snus constituents.

comparison.controls: People who never used tobacco, in each primary study.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level. Primary studies adjusted for different covariate sets (Table S2, not read).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Diet, alcohol, socio-economic position and occupational exposures differ between snus and no-tobacco groups in some cohorts; the authors judge occupational and socio-economic confounding in the construction-worker cohort to be small because workers are fairly uniform and two lung-cancer case-control studies there found little confounding by smoking (Discussion › 4.2, 6th paragraph); this is argument, not measurement.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Alcohol is not discussed as a confounder in the main text. Smoking is handled by restriction.

outcomes.instruments: Cancer incidence by site from cancer registers (oral cavity, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, colon, rectum, anus, lung, lymphoma, leukaemia and myeloma, melanoma, any cancer), total mortality, cancer-specific mortality, and mortality after a cancer diagnosis.
outcomes.validity_norms: Register-based outcomes. Risk of bias in the primary studies was rated moderate for all, mostly because of the validity of the exposure information (Results › 3.1, 3rd paragraph; Table S5, not read).
outcomes.operationalization: Harm is cancer or death against never use of tobacco, as hazard, risk or incidence rate ratios. Confidence is graded by GRADE: observational evidence starts low, upgraded to moderate for estimates above 2.0 or below 0.5, and graded very low when the interval spans both harm and benefit.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable. About 15 cancer or mortality outcomes are graded or reported; no correction for multiple outcomes, and each rests on one study.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Study selection was done by two researchers independently at both stages; data extraction by one author and checked by another; risk of bias assessed and discussed by two researchers.

analysis.effect_sizes: GRADE table (Table 1), snus only against no tobacco, relative effect with absolute risk with and without snus per 100,000 over each study's follow-up: oral cancer HR 0.93 (0.59 to 1.44), 90 against 84, very low certainty; oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma HR 3.5 (1.6 to 7.6), 16 against 55, moderate; non-cardia stomach cancer HR 1.4 (1.1 to 1.9), 237 against 332, low; pancreatic cancer, 27 years of follow-up, RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.3 in the table, 1.2 to 3.6 in the text), 72 against 151, moderate; pancreatic cancer, 36 years, HR 1.07 (0.77 to 1.50), 225 against 241, very low; rectal cancer HR 1.38 (1.07 to 1.77), 339 against 468, low; rectal cancer pooled with a longer follow-up of the main cohort HR 1.10 (0.91 to 1.34), low; cancer-specific mortality HR 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26), 2,141 against 2,395, low. Not graded: lung cancer RR 0.8 (0.4 to 1.3, 15 exposed cases); colon cancer HR 1.08 (0.91 to 1.29); anal cancer HR 0.61 (0.07 to 5.07, 1 case); non-Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.77 (0.59 to 1.01); Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.88 (0.49 to 1.58); leukaemias and myeloma IRRs 0.81 to 1.24; all melanoma IRR 0.65 (0.52 to 0.82); any cancer in never-smoking men HR 1.1 (0.9 to 1.4); smoking-related cancers HR 1.6 (1.1 to 2.5). Mortality: all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20 to 1.35) from the pooled Swedish analysis, 1.23 (1.09 to 1.40) in a separate cohort; after any cancer diagnosis, total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05 to 1.20) and cancer death HR 1.15 (1.05 to 1.26); after prostate cancer, overall HR 1.19 (1.04 to 1.37) and prostate cancer death HR 1.24 (1.03 to 1.49); after colorectal cancer, overall HR 1.16 (0.89 to 1.50).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; studies of never-smoking men were chosen so that smoking would not need adjustment. Some primary studies adjusted for cancer site, age and other factors (Table S2, not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021293500 is cited; the article read gives no statement on deviations from the registered protocol, and the registration itself was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: GRADE rows were chosen for cancers with a graded estimate; ungraded outcomes (lymphoma, leukaemia, myeloma, melanoma) are reported in text. Where several studies shared a population, the largest or longest was graded and, for pancreatic and rectal cancer, an earlier shorter-follow-up result was also shown. The abstract and conclusions foreground the increased estimates (oesophagus, pancreas, stomach, rectum) and give less weight to the null or lower estimates (oral cancer, lung cancer, lymphoma, melanoma, colon cancer).
analysis.power: Low for rare cancers, as the authors say. Examples: oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 10 exposed cases; oral cancer 25; anal cancer 1; pancreatic cancer 18 exposed cases at 27 years.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 15 mostly Swedish, mostly male, observational studies, men who used snus only did not clearly differ from men who never used tobacco in oral cancer (HR 0.93, 0.59 to 1.44), lung cancer (RR 0.8, 0.4 to 1.3) or colon cancer (HR 1.08, 0.91 to 1.29). Higher estimates were reported for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (HR 3.5, 1.6 to 7.6, 10 exposed cases), non-cardia stomach cancer (HR 1.4, 1.1 to 1.9), pancreatic cancer at 27 years (RR 2.1, 1.2 to 3.3) and rectal cancer (HR 1.38, 1.07 to 1.77), each from one study; at longer follow-up the pancreatic estimate fell to HR 1.07 (0.77 to 1.50) and the rectal estimate to 1.10 (0.91 to 1.34) when pooled with a longer follow-up of the main cohort. Cancer-specific death was slightly higher (HR 1.12, lower limit 1.00) and so was death after a cancer diagnosis (HR 1.13 to 1.19). Melanoma was lower (IRR 0.65). Certainty ranged from moderate (oesophagus, pancreas at 27 years) to very low.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says snus probably increases the risk of cancer of the oesophagus and pancreas, may increase the risk of stomach and rectal cancer, and that the evidence suggests more cancer-specific deaths; it concludes snus entails a cancer hazard whose size may depend on a person's history of use and susceptibility. Gaps: (1) causal verbs ('increases') rest on one observational study each, with 10 exposed cases for the oesophagus and 18 for the pancreas at 27 years; (2) the larger, longer pancreatic analysis (36 years) was rated very low and showed no clear difference, and the rectal estimate fell from 1.38 to 1.10 with 10 more years of follow-up, yet the abstract and conclusions list rectal and pancreatic cancer among the increased risks and the Discussion says there is reason to believe a causal link exists for rectal cancer; (3) all studies were rated at moderate risk of bias for exposure information, but this did not lead to any downgrade in the GRADE table, and the oesophagus is rated moderate although the footnote says it was downgraded for few events; (4) the conclusion is stated as 'hazard' (whether snus can cause cancer), not as the size of a person's risk, and no results are given for women; (5) the section comparing snus with smoking is descriptive, built from separate studies in one figure that was not read here.

timeline.event: Norwegian Knowledge Centre for the Health Services report, the first search (2004) on which this review's search builds.
Norwegian Institute of Public Health update (search 2013); a further update followed in 2019 (search 2018).
Pooled analysis of nine Swedish cohorts on oral cancer, the most recent study used for the oral cancer grade (as stated in the Results).
Pooled analysis of eight Swedish cohorts on mortality, whose cancer-specific death estimate (HR 1.12) is the review's mortality row.
This review (search May 2022); the authors say its findings agree with earlier evaluations by IARC and the US National Cancer Institute.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent systematic review of snus and cancer identified. Its findings overlap heavily with the pooled analysis of mortality (byhamre_2021) and with each other (the same construction-worker cohort contributes to most estimates), so the estimates are not independent replications. The oesophageal and pancreatic findings rest on one study each and have not been confirmed in a second independent cohort in this review; the pancreatic estimate shrank with longer follow-up.

funding.funder: Not stated in the page text read (the article has a conflict-of-interest statement and an acknowledgement for the librarian, but no funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: All the authors declare no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health (Divisions of Climate and Environmental Health and for Health Services), the Nordic Institute of Dental Materials, the University of Oslo, the National Institute of Occupational Health and the Cancer Registry of Norway. The review excluded primary studies by researchers with a link to the tobacco industry or sponsored by it; the text read does not say which studies were excluded for that reason (Table S4 not read). The other review of snus and health in this batch (lee_2013), by a long-term consultant to the tobacco industry and supported by a snus manufacturer, reads an earlier body of evidence (to 2012) more reassuringly.

what_would_settle_it: Several independent, large cohorts of snus-only and never-tobacco men, women included, with tobacco use recorded repeatedly through follow-up (so quitting and switching to smoking are counted), and site-specific cancers followed beyond age 70, pooled with individual participant data so that each cancer site rests on more than one population; plus cancer-site studies of people who switched from smoking to snus, which were excluded here.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people using snus only), exposure, comparator (never use of tobacco), outcomes (cancer, mortality) and designs are specified.
PROSPERO CRD42021293500 is cited; the article does not describe deviations, and the registered protocol was not read.
Eligibility says there was no restriction on design; no reason is given for including cohort and case-control studies (only observational evidence exists for this question).

Six databases searched by a librarian, built on three earlier searches, with reference lists screened and the search within 24 months of publication; but language limited to English and three Scandinavian languages without a justification, no grey literature, no trial or study registries and no content experts mentioned. Judged 'no' because AMSTAR 2 item 4 is applied as written (unjustified publication restriction), as for every card of earlier batches (decision p-amstar2-item4). The search strategy itself is in a supplement not read.
Two researchers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently; disagreements were resolved by discussion.

One author extracted and another checked that the right information was extracted; authors of primary studies were contacted for missing data. Meets the item's first criterion as read in earlier cards of this project (two reviewers reaching consensus).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the text says excluded studies are listed with reasons in Table S4; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The main text gives, for each study, the outcome, comparison, number of exposed cases and often follow-up and cohort; effect estimates, characteristics of the snus groups and confounder adjustments are in Table S2 (not read); the text does not describe setting and follow-up for every study.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Joanna Briggs Institute checklists for cohort and case-control studies, assessed and discussed by two researchers, covering confounding, selection and exposure and outcome measurement; the checklists do not cover selection of the reported result, and the study-level ratings are in Table S5 (not read). All studies were rated moderate risk of bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported in the main text; Table S2, which lists other study details, was not read. The review did screen for industry links and sponsorship at eligibility.

The only pooling is a generic inverse-variance combination of two adjusted hazard ratios for rectal cancer from non-overlapping parts of the same collaboration (the non-construction cohorts and the longer follow-up of the construction cohort); it is appropriate for that purpose, though the model and heterogeneity are not stated.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No meaningful quantitative synthesis: one two-study pooling, with all studies rated the same (moderate) risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion (4.2) analyses how single baseline recording of exposure, misclassification of smoking and cohort features could affect estimates and says why smoking was handled by restriction; but the moderate risk of bias did not lead to a GRADE downgrade.

Differences between estimates for the same cancer are examined (time-varying hazard ratios for pancreatic and rectal cancer across follow-up periods, with a shorter and a longer follow-up of the same cohort).
No meaningful quantitative synthesis, so no test is possible; the Discussion does not address publication bias or selective reporting qualitatively.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The authors declare no conflicts of interest; the funding of the review is not stated in the page text read.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: AMSTAR 2 rates one critical item as 'no' (item 4: an unjustified language restriction and no other sources beyond databases and reference lists), and item 7 is provisional because Table S4 was not read; if that list does not give reasons, the rating becomes critically low. Items 2 and 9 are partly met. The review is registered, uses duplicate screening, a standard bias checklist and GRADE, and writes its uncertainty out, so its estimates are best cited as a transparent, graded summary of a small observational literature that is dominated by one cohort and one sex. It may be cited for the site-by-site estimates and their certainty, the absolute risks in its GRADE table, the shrinking of the pancreatic and rectal estimates with longer follow-up, and the absence of data on women; not for causal statements, for any comparison with smoking beyond what is stated, or for independent replication.

key_findings.finding: 2,450 records screened, 67 read in full, 15 studies included (14 cohort studies, 1 case-control study); all rated moderate risk of bias, mostly for the validity of exposure information. Only one study reported any estimate for women (lymphoma, no cases).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › 3.1 Cancer risk of snus use compared with no tobacco use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Graded estimates, snus only against no tobacco (Table 1): oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma HR 3.5 (1.6 to 7.6) from one cohort study of 142,891 men, 16 against 55 cases per 100,000, moderate certainty; non-cardia stomach cancer HR 1.4 (1.1 to 1.9), 237 against 332 per 100,000, low; rectal cancer HR 1.38 (1.07 to 1.77), 339 against 468 per 100,000, low; pancreatic cancer at 27 years RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.3 in the table), 72 against 151 per 100,000, moderate; oral cancer HR 0.93 (0.59 to 1.44), very low; cancer-specific mortality HR 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26), 2,141 against 2,395 per 100,000, low.

Pancreatic cancer in the Construction Workers Cohort varied with the length of follow-up: HR 1.98 (0.97 to 4.03, 4 exposed cases) to 1994, 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6, 18 cases) to 2004, 1.34 (0.90 to 1.99, 31 cases) to 2013; the pooled nine-cohort analysis (36 years, 41 exposed cases) gave HR 1.07 (0.77 to 1.50), graded very low. In that pooled analysis two thirds of participants and 72% of cases or deaths came from the Construction Workers Cohort.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.4 Cancer of the pancreas, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure 2 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Rectal cancer: HR 1.38 (1.07 to 1.77, 73 exposed cases) at 27 years of follow-up in nine pooled cohorts; combining the non-construction cohorts with a 10-years-longer follow-up of the Construction Workers Cohort gave HR 1.10 (0.91 to 1.34), a drop of almost 20% in the point estimate. Colon cancer HR 1.02 to 1.08 and anal cancer 0.61 (0.07 to 5.07, 1 case) showed no clear difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1.5 Cancer of the colon, rectum and anus, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 3 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Estimates close to no difference or lower: oral cancer (pooled 9 cohorts HR 0.93, 0.59 to 1.44, 25 exposed cases; a third study of oral and pharyngeal cancers combined HR 2.3, 0.7 to 8.3, 5 cases), lung cancer RR 0.8 (0.4 to 1.3, 15 cases), non-Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.77 (0.59 to 1.01), Hodgkin lymphoma IRR 0.88 (0.49 to 1.58), leukaemias and myeloma IRR 0.81 to 1.24, all melanoma IRR 0.65 (0.52 to 0.82); lymphoma, leukaemia and melanoma results were not graded because they were given as incidence rate ratios.

Mortality: pooled Swedish analysis all-cause HR 1.28 (1.20 to 1.35) and cancer-specific HR 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26); a separate cohort not in that analysis, HR 1.23 (1.09 to 1.40) for all-cause and 1.28 (0.96 to 1.69) for cancer death in never-smoking men who had ever used snus. After a cancer diagnosis in construction workers, total mortality HR 1.13 (1.05 to 1.20) and cancer death HR 1.15 (1.05 to 1.26); after prostate cancer, overall HR 1.19 (1.04 to 1.37) and prostate cancer death HR 1.24 (1.03 to 1.49); after colorectal cancer, overall HR 1.16 (0.89 to 1.50), and 1.89 (1.21 to 2.94, 22 deaths) when the construction cohort was left out.

The authors' summary: snus probably increases the risk of cancer of the oesophagus and pancreas (moderate certainty), may increase the risk of stomach and rectal cancer (low), and the evidence suggests more cancer deaths and more deaths after a cancer diagnosis (low); they are very uncertain about the other cancers, and do not know the effect in women. They conclude snus entails a cancer hazard whose size may depend on a person's history of use and host susceptibility.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph; Summary of evidence for cancer risk

key_findings.finding: Smoking comparison: where smoking and snus were compared against the same never-tobacco group in the same studies, cancer risk estimates were higher for smoking than for snus at most sites, and all confidence intervals overlapped except for lung cancer; the figure with the estimates (Figure 4) was not read as numbers. The authors say it is not known how much switching from smoking to snus would reduce the benefit expected from quitting all tobacco.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.5 (snus compared with cigarettes), 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Figure 4 (values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Exposure caveats: a single baseline recording of tobacco habits; about 30% of men using snus only may later stop or switch to smoking (a Swedish study cited); more than 75% of men using snus only were under 30 at entry and few were followed beyond 70; seven of the included studies used construction-worker data from 1971 to 1975, when non-use could not be told from non-response; 13.2% of never-smoking men using snus, against 6.7% of men who never used tobacco, had a repeat record showing smoking, though the authors cite a sensitivity analysis in which 60% of the snus group would have to be smokers to shift one oesophageal result.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › 4.2 Impact of exposure information, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Tobacco-industry studies were excluded by design; studies reporting only dual use of snus and cigarettes were also excluded; the review states that adjusting for smoking in samples that included smokers distorted snus estimates in one study.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.3 Study eligibility criteria; Discussion › 4.1 Grading the results, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the pancreatic cancer estimate at 27 years is printed as RR 2.1 (1.2 to 3.3); the text prints the same estimate as 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6) twice. The table's absolute risk (151 per 100,000, upper limit 237) matches an upper limit of 3.3 (72 x 3.3 = 238).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1; Results › 3.1.4, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limit is uncertain by 0.3. IARC Monograph 100E (sc_iarc_2012) prints the Swedish construction-worker cohort's never-smoker pancreatic estimate as 2.1 (1.2 to 3.6; 18 cases), which agrees with the text of this review; the primary study has not been checked. The industry-linked review in this batch (Lee 2013) prints what appears to be the same study's never-smoker estimate as 2.00 (1.20 to 3.30), so the point estimate also differs (2.0 against 2.1).

reporting_issues.issue: The bracketed numbers in Table 1's absolute-risk column are the confidence limits of the risk with snus (for example oral cancer 53 to 130 per 100,000 around 84), but they are labelled 'fewer' and 'more' as if they were differences from the no-tobacco risk of 90.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader who takes '53 fewer to 130 more' as a difference would be misled; the claim should quote the risks with and without snus, not the bracketed words.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 attributes the oral cancer, 36-year pancreatic cancer and rectal cancer estimates all to 'Araghi et al' with the same reference number (18), while the text cites different reference numbers for these (25 for oral cancer, 23 for pancreatic cancer, 18 for colorectal cancer) and uses both 18 and 23 for the rectal cancer estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The three estimates come from different papers by the same group; the reference list must be checked before any is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The oesophageal estimate is rated moderate and footnote b says it was downgraded for very few events, while the review's own rule starts observational evidence at low and upgrades to moderate for an estimate above 2.0; a downgrade after an upgrade would give low.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 footnote b; Methods › 2.6, after Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The certainty for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma may be one level lower than printed; Table S3 (not read) holds the reasoning.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists stomach cancer as one study, the Results describe two (a case-control study and the cohort study), and the Discussion refers to 14 included studies where the Results count 15.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract; Results › 3.1.3; Discussion › 4.2, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor counting inconsistency; the case-control stomach result (OR 0.5, 0.2 to 1.2) is lower than the cohort result and is not part of the graded estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The cancer-specific mortality row cites 163,412 participants, whereas the source paper analysed 169,103 men; the difference of 5,691 equals the number of men who formerly used snus there.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (cancer-specific mortality row); compare sc_byhamre_2021
reporting_issues.consequence: Explained by counting only the two groups compared; the same estimate and its overlap with the mortality paper must not be counted twice in a claim.
